notes: Wilson governs alone (Labour majority since 1966); the template coalition slot 18 holds the Tribune Group, the organised Labour left, as the nearest partner. Ulster Unionists sit in slot 14 as the regional conservative party. SNP and Plaid Cymru are not placed. All icons null: the only tag sprite (ENG_nat_populism) belongs to Reform UK.

0.name: Security Service
0.text:
The Security Service is Britain's domestic counter-intelligence agency, headed since 1965 by Sir Martin Furnival Jones. Still scarred by the Cambridge spy scandals, a hard core of its officers, Peter Wright among them, has absorbed the defector Anatoliy Golitsyn's theories of Soviet penetration and regards Harold Wilson's circle with open suspicion.

The Service sees itself as the guardian of the realm against communist subversion in the unions, the Labour left and the universities, working closely with the CIA and the FBI. Its leverage lies in secret files, telephone taps and the ear of senior civil servants; in a crisis its officers could become the backbone of an authoritarian, firmly Atlanticist emergency order.

1.name: Conservative and Unionist Party
1.text:
The Conservative and Unionist Party is Britain's traditional party of government, out of office since 1964 and led since 1965 by Edward Heath, a grammar-school technocrat who has modernised its machinery. Leading the polls after devaluation and Labour's battles with the unions, it prepares to fight the next general election.

Heath promises tax cuts, a legal framework for industrial relations, an end to subsidising lame-duck industries and, above all, British entry into the European Economic Community. The party is staunchly pro-NATO and Atlanticist. Its base lies in the shires, the suburbs, the City and the professions, while Enoch Powell's dismissal from the shadow cabinet in 1968 leaves a restless populist right inside its ranks.

2.name: Liberal Party
2.text:
The Liberal Party, once the great rival of the Conservatives, survives as a small third force with a dozen MPs, concentrated in the Celtic fringe and rural constituencies. Since 1967 it has been led by the flamboyant Jeremy Thorpe, while the Young Liberals, the Red Guards, embarrass the leadership with radical campaigns against apartheid and the Vietnam War.

Liberals call for electoral reform, devolution, worker co-ownership, civil liberties and enthusiastic British membership of the European Community. Firmly Western but critical of Cold War rigidity, the party appeals to nonconformist voters, protest voters and the educated middle class, and its leverage lies in by-election upsets and in any hung parliament.

3.name: Labour Party
3.text:
The Labour Party has governed Britain since 1964 under Harold Wilson, who won a majority of nearly a hundred seats in 1966. Its government has survived the 1967 devaluation of sterling and the abandonment of Barbara Castle's union reform plan In Place of Strife, and Roy Jenkins' austere budgets are restoring a balance of payments surplus.

Built on the trade unions affiliated to it, Labour promises planning, the white heat of technological change, comprehensive schools and a modern welfare state. Wilson keeps Britain loyal to NATO and close to Washington while refusing troops for Vietnam. Its strength lies in the industrial heartlands, Scotland and Wales, but strikes and rising prices test its claim to manage the economy.

4.name: Communist Party of Great Britain
4.text:
The Communist Party of Great Britain, founded in 1920, is led by General Secretary John Gollan and publishes the daily Morning Star. It holds no seats in Parliament and polls only a few thousand votes, yet in August 1968 it broke with tradition by condemning the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The party follows The British Road to Socialism, a parliamentary strategy for a left-wing government backed by mass struggle, and remains close to Moscow in foreign policy. Its real strength lies in industry, where its militants and its industrial organiser Bert Ramelson hold key posts in engineering, mining and docks unions and coordinate shop stewards against wage restraint.

5.name: International Marxist Group
5.text:
The International Marxist Group is the British section of the Fourth International, renamed in 1968 and propelled by the student revolt. Its best-known member, the Pakistani-born orator Tariq Ali, led the Vietnam Solidarity Campaign marches on the American embassy in Grosvenor Square, and the paper Black Dwarf spread its ideas on campus.

The IMG preaches permanent revolution, international solidarity with Vietnam and the Third World, and a break with Labour reformism. It regards students and young workers as the vanguard of a coming European upheaval inspired by Paris in May 1968. Small in numbers, it punches above its weight through demonstrations, occupations and its talent for capturing headlines.

6.name: Union Movement
6.text:
The Union Movement was founded in 1948 by Sir Oswald Mosley, the pre-war leader of the British Union of Fascists. After poor results in 1966 Mosley withdrew to France, leaving his loyal lieutenant Jeffrey Hamm to keep a dwindling organisation alive in London's East End and in the pages of its paper Action.

Its creed, Europe a Nation, rejects both American capitalism and Soviet communism and calls for a united white Europe as a third superpower, with Africa as its partner. Hostile to Washington, NATO and Wall Street, it campaigns against Commonwealth immigration. Its remaining leverage lies in old fascist networks and in sympathy among disillusioned imperial nationalists.

7.name: The Tankies
7.text:
The Tankies are the hardline minority of British communists who applauded the Soviet tanks in Budapest in 1956 and in Prague in 1968. Their stronghold is the CPGB's Surrey District under its secretary Sid French, which openly defies the party leadership's condemnation of the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

They regard the Soviet Union as the unquestionable centre of world socialism and denounce the drift towards parliamentary reformism. Their ideal is a disciplined vanguard state on the Soviet model, allied with Moscow and the Warsaw Pact. Their leverage lies in old party cadres, friendship societies and Soviet sympathy, and they would be Moscow's natural partners in any authoritarian socialist order.

8.name: Shia Imami Ismaili Muslim Community
8.text:
The Shia Imami Ismaili community in Britain is growing quickly as Asian families from Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda settle in London and the Midlands. They follow Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, their Harvard-educated hereditary imam since 1957, who directs a dense network of councils, schools, clinics and businesses.

The community embodies a reformist, outward-looking Shia Islam that stresses education, enterprise, women's participation and loyalty to the host country. Wary of revolutionary politics, it favours gradual modernisation of Muslim societies and close ties with Western institutions. Its leverage lies in wealth, organisation and the Aga Khan's international prestige, which open doors in Whitehall and across the Commonwealth.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party is a clandestine Iraqi Shia movement formed in Najaf in the late 1950s by young clerics around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Since the Ba'ath regime's campaign against the Najaf seminaries in 1969, its members face arrest and torture, and Iraqi Shia students, doctors and merchants in London quietly carry its ideas abroad.

Da'wa calls for an Islamic state guided by the Shia clergy, rejecting both Western liberalism and Ba'athist socialism, and seeks to rebuild society on Islamic economics and law. Its cells are secretive and disciplined. In Britain its leverage is small, resting on student societies, mosques and contacts with the great clerical families of Najaf and Karbala.

10.name: Islamic Cultural Centre, Regent's Park
10.text:
The Islamic Cultural Centre in Regent's Park was opened in 1944 on land granted by King George VI, in exchange for a site given to the British in Cairo. Run by a trust of ambassadors from Muslim states, with Saudi Arabia and the Gulf monarchies increasingly influential, it is preparing to build London's Central Mosque.

The Centre represents official, conservative Sunni Islam: Friday prayers, marriages, halal certification and religious instruction under the patronage of friendly governments. It shuns radical politics and treats loyalty to the British state and to the Muslim monarchies as complementary. Its leverage lies in diplomatic backing, oil money and its standing as the face of Islam to the British establishment.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and is banned throughout the Arab world for its attempts to win over army officers. Hunted by the security services of Jordan, Syria and Iraq, its members find refuge among Arab and Pakistani students at British universities.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, demanding the restoration of a single caliphate that would unite the Islamic world and confront both Western and Soviet power. It works through intellectual study circles and leaflets rather than open violence. In Britain its leverage is minimal, but its disciplined cadres plant ideas among a new generation.

12.name: UK Islamic Mission
12.text:
The UK Islamic Mission was founded in 1962 by Pakistani immigrants inspired by Abul A'la Mawdudi and the Jamaat-e-Islami. Alongside the Federation of Student Islamic Societies, which links Muslim students across British campuses, it is building mosques, supplementary schools and study circles in the industrial towns of England and Scotland.

The Mission promotes Islam as a complete way of life and seeks to protect immigrant families from secular British culture through education and community work. It cooperates with the Muslim Brotherhood's networks abroad, but in Britain it works lawfully and patiently. Its leverage lies in its organisation among Pakistani communities and in its growing role as their voice.

13.name: National Emergency Government
13.text:
The idea of a National Emergency Government is the obsession of Cecil King, the newspaper magnate dismissed as chairman of the International Publishing Corporation in 1968. In May 1968 he sounded out Lord Mountbatten about leading a government of businessmen, generals and experts to replace Wilson, a proposal the scientific adviser Solly Zuckerman flatly rejected.

Its sympathisers believe that party politics, union power and sterling crises are dragging Britain into decline and that only an emergency administration above parties can restore order. Neither Atlanticist nor anti-Western, it is a plan of national salvation. Its leverage lies in boardrooms, Fleet Street and a few retired officers, waiting for a crisis.

14.name: Ulster Unionist Party
14.text:
The Ulster Unionist Party has governed Northern Ireland from Stormont since 1921. Its leader and Northern Ireland Prime Minister, James Chichester-Clark, took over from Terence O'Neill in 1969 and now presides over a province under British troops after the August riots, while his party splits between reformers and hardliners.

The party defends the Union, the Protestant ascendancy in local government and its intimate ties with the Orange Order. At Westminster its MPs take the Conservative whip, but in Belfast it is a separate force. Its leverage lies in Stormont's control of police and patronage, and in its ability to mobilise loyalist crowds.

15.name: Confederation of British Industry
15.text:
The Confederation of British Industry was formed in 1965 by merging the employers' federations into a single voice of business, and since 1969 Campbell Adamson has served as its Director-General. It speaks for the great manufacturing firms, the nationalised industries' suppliers and the City institutions behind them.

The CBI wants restraint on wages, curbs on unofficial strikes, lower taxation and entry into the Common Market, while accepting a role in tripartite planning with government and the unions. Its leverage lies in investment decisions, its seats on public bodies and the close links its members enjoy with ministers of both parties and with the Bank of England.

16.name: Institute of Economic Affairs
16.text:
The Institute of Economic Affairs was founded in 1955 by the businessman Antony Fisher on the advice of Friedrich Hayek. Run by Ralph Harris and Arthur Seldon, it publishes a steady flow of pamphlets attacking the post-war consensus and courts a small band of Conservative politicians and economic journalists.

The IEA champions free markets, sound money, the end of exchange controls, choice in health and education through vouchers, and limits on trade union power. It sees Keynesian planning and nationalisation as the roots of British decline. Although outside the mainstream in 1970, its leverage lies in ideas: it is training the arguments a future Conservative right will use.

17.name: The Conservation Society
17.text:
The Conservation Society was founded in 1966 and has become Britain's first campaigning environmental organisation, attracting scientists, teachers and middle-class activists. In European Conservation Year 1970 it gains audiences for its warnings about pollution, motorways, pesticides and the exhaustion of natural resources.

The Society argues that unlimited economic and population growth is impossible on a finite planet, and calls for population stabilisation, recycling and a stable economy. It stands outside the Cold War blocs and criticises both capitalist and communist industrialism. Its leverage lies in expert testimony, local branches fighting road schemes and a public increasingly alarmed by oil spills like the Torrey Canyon disaster.

18.name: Tribune Group
18.text:
The Tribune Group is the organised left of the Parliamentary Labour Party, named after the weekly Tribune and including Michael Foot, Ian Mikardo, Eric Heffer and Frank Allaun. It harried the Wilson government over prescription charges, Vietnam and In Place of Strife, and helped defeat the union reform bill in 1969.

Tribunites demand wider public ownership, economic planning, an end to support for the American war in Vietnam, cuts in defence spending and, for many, unilateral nuclear disarmament. Sceptical of the Common Market, they want a socialist Britain independent of the superpowers. Their leverage lies in the constituency parties, the left-led unions and the votes they command on the backbenches.

19.name: International Socialists
19.text:
The International Socialists grew out of the Socialist Review Group founded by the Palestinian-born Marxist Tony Cliff. After 1968 the group expanded rapidly among students and young workers, adopting a Leninist structure and a weekly paper, Socialist Worker, while building rank-and-file groups in the factories.

IS holds that the Soviet Union is state capitalist and its slogan Neither Washington nor Moscow but International Socialism rejects both blocs. It calls for workers' control, rank-and-file union power and a revolutionary party independent of Labour. Its leverage lies in shop-floor militancy against incomes policy and in its ability to recruit the radicalised generation of 1968.

20.name: Conservative Monday Club
20.text:
The Monday Club was founded in 1961 by Conservatives outraged by Harold Macmillan's Wind of Change speech and the rapid end of empire. It has grown into the main pressure group of the Tory right, with MPs such as Patrick Wall and John Biggs-Davison and a membership swelled by sympathy for Enoch Powell after his 1968 immigration speech.

The Club opposes sanctions against Rhodesia, defends white rule in southern Africa, demands an end to coloured immigration with assisted repatriation, and calls for tougher law and order. Fiercely anti-communist and patriotic, it distrusts the European project. Its leverage lies in constituency associations and in the populist mood Powell has unleashed.

21.name: National Front
21.text:
The National Front was formed in 1967 by merging the League of Empire Loyalists, the British National Party and the Racial Preservation Society, later joined by John Tyndall's followers. Its chairman is the veteran writer A. K. Chesterton, a former Mosley propagandist, and it is preparing to field candidates at the next general election.

Behind a patriotic facade, its core leadership comes from Britain's neo-Nazi fringe. The Front demands the compulsory repatriation of immigrants, the restoration of empire, withdrawal from international bodies and an end to the alleged power of international finance. It recruits disaffected white workers and frustrated Conservatives, and its leverage lies in street mobilisation around immigration.

22.name: Chiefs of Staff Committee
22.text:
The Chiefs of Staff Committee unites the professional heads of the Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force under the Chief of the Defence Staff, Marshal of the Royal Air Force Sir Charles Elworthy. The armed forces are withdrawing from east of Suez while British troops have patrolled the streets of Northern Ireland since August 1969.

The officer corps is loyal to the Crown and politically discreet, but resents defence cuts, union disorder and what many see as weak government. Should the state face civil breakdown, the services would become the guarantors of order, ruling through emergency powers. Their leverage lies in their monopoly of force and their prestige with the establishment.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
The House of Windsor has reigned since 1917, and Queen Elizabeth II has been sovereign since 1952. In 1969 the investiture of Prince Charles as Prince of Wales and the documentary Royal Family brought the monarchy closer to the public, while Lord Mountbatten remains a forceful voice behind the scenes.

The Crown is constitutionally above politics, yet it retains reserve powers to appoint a prime minister and dissolve Parliament, and commands the loyalty of the armed forces and much of the Commonwealth. A royalist government would invoke these prerogatives to stand above discredited parties. Its leverage lies in deep popular affection and in its symbolic authority.
